newsitem.title: USA: Fran's victims share the storm by phone and tv.
newsitem.headline: Fran's victims share the storm by phone and tv.

text.p: As Hurricane Fran caved in their homes and chased snakes onto their porches, media-savvy residents of this North Carolina city jumped to their telephones, becoming reporters of their own disaster.

The storm whipped through the darkened city of Wilmington with 100 mph (160 kmh) winds and torrential rains, tumbling trees and collapsing roofs. But some undaunted victims, eyeing a chance at brief notoriety, jostled to get on the air at local television stations.

"It's pretty rough out here. The wind blew a tree over on the roof and it knocked the chimney in, so we've got bricks coming down the fireplace," a woman who identifed herself as Beth Howell said on WECT, an NBC affiliate. "It's really wild outside."

The play-by-play desciptions of Fran's passage recalled those of four years ago in southern Florida, when Hurricane Andrew tore through the Miami area, leaving more than $20 billion in damage in its wake.

During that storm, which made landfall after 4 a.m. (0800 GMT), dozens of residents called local stations on their cellular telephones as they cowered in closets and bathrooms while the deadly Category 4 storm tore apart their homes.
As Fran bore down on Wilmington at nightfall, edgy residents used telephones and television to vent frustrations, report accidents and let kinfolk know they were okay.
"There's about three feet of water around us," Donna Ludlow told WECT from the second floor of a home in Carolina Beach. "In case my sister is listening, we're fine. Her property is under water."
For some residents, the storm provided a chance to do some ad-lib news reporting as they took the role of journalists who long before had sought safe shelter as the storm's winds rose.

"I'm back here looking out the rear window of the patio. I'm opening the door now," said Rick Ryan, of Fayetteville. "It looks like we're really getting bombarded. I don't know if you can hear this or not."
"We saw a car go by here -- floating that is," said another caller who telephoned from Carolina Beach.
From the mundane to the bizzare, hurricane victims seemed delighted with the chance to tell their stories in real time.
"There's probably 15 to 18 snakes out there on my porch," Jim Johnstone said from Rocky Point. "I've got hundreds of green frogs on the porch too."
